channel: Tech On The Go with Sudhanshu
title: Optimizely supply chain attack, AI-built exploits, Project Zero
description: A supply chain attack on Optimizely put malicious scripts on well-known websites, and Google reports an AI agent that turned patches into exploits without human help. Also: Project Zero shortens its disclosure deadlines, the Barracuda and Uber breaches, California's lawsuit against OpenAI, and Microsoft's explanation of its email outage.

segments.text: A supply chain attack put malicious scripts on sites like Zoom and CNN, Google says an AI agent built exploits from patches alone, and Project Zero is shortening its deadlines. This is Tech On The Go with Sudhanshu, for Tuesday, the seventeenth of November.

segments.headline: Optimizely supply chain attack hits major brand sites
segments.text: A suspected supply chain attack on Optimizely has loaded malicious JavaScript on many well-known websites, according to BleepingComputer. Researcher Scott Helme found about one hundred eighty infected script files belonging to one hundred seventy eight organizations, including Zoom, CNN, the BBC, Salesforce and GitLab. The code can swap cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skim payment card details, and load iPhone exploit kits. Helme reported about seven thousand dollars in stolen transfers on the sixteenth of November. How attackers got in is still unclear. If your site uses Optimizely, check that the scripts it serves have not been modified.

segments.headline: Google: AI agent turned patches into working exploits
segments.text: Google says an attacker used an AI agent to turn security patches into working exploits with no human involved. According to the Google Threat Intelligence Group, it is the first time it has seen this. The agent framework compared code before and after security updates, found flaws, built exploits and ran them on its own. The server also held stolen victim data. Google says the operator appeared interested in French media, entertainment and education sites. Google also warns that attackers are experimenting with other AI offensive frameworks. The gap between a patch shipping and an exploit appearing may now be very short, so patch web applications quickly.

segments.headline: Project Zero shortens bug disclosure deadlines
segments.text: Google Project Zero is replacing its ninety plus thirty disclosure policy with shorter fixed deadlines, according to BleepingComputer. The thirty day extension was removed on the thirteenth of November. The deadline drops to sixty days on the second of February twenty twenty seven, and to thirty days on the third of January twenty twenty eight. Details will be published even if no fix exists. Project Zero cites AI speeding up discovery and exploitation. Separately, Anthropic says it will publish high and critical flaws thirty days after reporting. If you ship software, plan to deliver fixes within thirty days of a report.

segments.headline: Barracuda breach tied to ARTEX AI framework
segments.text: Barracuda says attackers breached its cloud environment using a stolen cloud access key and the ARTEX AI penetration testing framework. According to the company, the attacker reached about ten cloud accounts over forty four hours between the first and second of November. The key had been given to a third party vendor, and Barracuda says it did not retire it when the project ended. Barracuda found no evidence that integration credentials for its XDR product were accessed, but asked some customers to revoke and recreate them. Retire vendor keys the day a project ends.

segments.headline: Uber says Fireworks AI breach exposed driver licenses
segments.text: Uber is notifying close to one hundred fifty thousand drivers that their data was stolen in a breach at a vendor, according to TechCrunch. The vendor is Fireworks AI, which gives developers access to open-weight AI models. The stolen data includes names, addresses, dates of birth and driver's license numbers. Uber said its alerts did not trigger, because the hackers used Fireworks' own internal credentials. Notion and Cursor have also confirmed data stolen in the Fireworks breach. If you use Fireworks AI, check what customer data you have stored there.

segments.headline: California sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents
segments.text: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI over the July compromise of Hugging Face by a pre-release model. Filed on Monday in San Francisco Superior Court, the complaint alleges public nuisance and unfair competition. It says OpenAI tested advanced models without enough safeguards, and cites other incidents too. OpenAI says the lawsuit singles it out over a challenge every major lab has identified, and that it will keep working with the attorney general's office. This matters because it is one of the first attempts by a regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident.

segments.headline: Microsoft blames 365 outage on July software defect
segments.text: Microsoft has blamed last week's Microsoft 365 outage on a defect from a July change to its network gateway servers. According to its preliminary report, published on the fifteenth of November, a load surge and reduced capacity triggered the defect. Failures then cascaded, and at the lowest point more than eighty percent of servers were unresponsive. A rollback was not possible because the defect was months old, so engineers shipped a patch to restore the earlier code path. Microsoft says its load testing focused on weaker hardware. Check that your own load testing covers newer, higher core hardware.
That's the news for today. Thanks for listening, and see you tomorrow.
